match.reason: The bank point teaches differentiation with the power rule, not the index laws for simplifying products and powers of exponents, so no bank point teaches the same idea.

draft.title: Index laws
card: A power a^n means n copies of a multiplied together. The small number n is the index, and a is the base.
Multiply
when the bases are the same, add the indices: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n). For example, 3² × 3⁴ = 3⁶.
Divide
when the bases are the same, subtract the indices: a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n). For example, 5⁷ ÷ 5³ = 5⁴.
Power of a power
multiply the indices: (a^m)^n = a^(mn). For example, (2³)² = 2⁶. Also a⁰ = 1, and a^(−n) = 1/a^n.
draft.remember: Same base: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide, multiply for a power of a power.

a.q: Which expression is equal to x⁵ × x³?
a.why: Same base, multiplying, so add the indices: 5 + 3 = 8. Multiplying the indices to get x¹⁵ is the rule for a power of a power, not for a product.
a.clue: The bases match and you are multiplying.

b.why: (2x³)² = 2² × x⁶ = 4x⁶, because both the 2 and the x³ are squared. Then 4x⁶ × x⁴ = 4x¹⁰. Leaving the 2 unsquared gives 2x¹⁰, which is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: The square applies to the 2 as well as to x³.

problems.detail: The question needs the power-of-a-product rule, (ab)^n = a^n b^n, to square the coefficient 2. The card never teaches this rule. Only the clue hints at it, so a student relying on the card alone may not know to square the 2.

'a⁰ = 1' and 'a^(−n) = 1/a^n' are stated without the condition a ≠ 0. Also, the opening definition of a power as 'n copies of a multiplied together' only works for positive whole-number n, yet the same card then uses zero and negative indices without noting this.

check.summary: Both intended answers are correct and unique. However, question b relies on the power-of-a-product rule (squaring the 2), which the card does not teach. The card also states a⁰ = 1 and a^(−n) = 1/a^n without the condition a ≠ 0.

proposal.title: Index laws
card: For a positive whole number n, a^n means n copies of the base a multiplied together. The number n is the index.
Multiply or divide
with the same base, add the indices to multiply and subtract them to divide: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) and a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n). For example, 3² × 3⁴ = 3⁶ and 5⁷ ÷ 5³ = 5⁴.
Power of a power
multiply the indices: (a^m)^n = a^(mn). For example, (2³)² = 2⁶.
Power of a product
raise every factor inside the brackets to the power: (ab)^n = a^n × b^n. For example, (3x²)² = 3² × x⁴ = 9x⁴.
proposal.remember: Same base: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide. A power outside brackets applies to every factor inside.

final.title: Index laws
card: For a positive whole number \(n\), \(a^{n}\) means \(n\) copies of the base \(a\) multiplied together. The number \(n\) is the index.
Multiply or divide

with the same base, add the indices to multiply and subtract them to divide: \(a^{m} \times a^{n} = a^{m + n}\) and \(a^{m} \div a^{n} = a^{m - n}\). For example, \(3^{2} \times 3^{4} = 3^{6}\) and \(5^{7} \div 5^{3} = 5^{4}\).
Power of a power
multiply the indices: \((a^{m})^{n} = a^{mn}\). For example, \((2^{3})^{2} = 2^{6}\).
Power of a product
raise every factor inside the brackets to the power: \((ab)^{n} = a^{n} \times b^{n}\). For example, \((3x^{2})^{2} = 3^{2} \times x^{4} = 9x^{4}\).
final.remember: Same base: add indices to multiply, subtract to divide. A power outside brackets applies to every factor inside.

a.q: Which expression is equal to \(x^{5} \times x^{3}\)?
a.why: Same base, multiplying, so add the indices: \(5 + 3 = 8\). Multiplying the indices to get \(x^{15}\) is the rule for a power of a power, not for a product.
a.clue: The bases match and you are multiplying.

b.why: Every factor in the brackets is squared: \((2x^{3})^{2} = 2^{2} \times x^{6} = 4x^{6}\). Then \(4x^{6} \times x^{4} = 4x^{10}\). Leaving the 2 unsquared gives \(2x^{10}\), which is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: Every factor inside the brackets is squared.
